secondary_method_note: solar_only counts every hour of winter sun as a heating penalty, whether or not the building needs heat then. Athens's winter sun is 2.8x London's (237.1 vs 85.2 kWh/m2), so this framing charges Athens a winter penalty of 111.7 vs 52.2 kWh/m2. Same data, opposite conclusions: solar_only ranks London first on net benefit, demand_weighted ranks Athens first. We use demand_weighted because kept-out sunlight only costs or saves energy in hours when the building needs heating or cooling.

methods.demand_weighted: Sunlight no longer absorbed = hourly global horizontal irradiation x (coated albedo - current median albedo), counted as benefit in hours above 24.0 C (cooling degree-hours) and as penalty in hours below 15.5 C (heating degree-hours), over summer and winter.
methods.solar_only: The same kept-out sunlight with all summer hours as benefit and all winter hours as penalty, regardless of heating or cooling demand.

heat_reference.text: Hottest hour of summer 2026 at the London reference point: 36.0 C (Open-Meteo). London reached 40 C in the July 2022 heatwave; that figure is from 2022, not 2026.

conclusion: Primary method (demand_weighted): London's heating need is 2.1x Athens's (19188 vs 9270 heating degree-hours below 15.5 C), and the coating's net return there is lower: 115.0 vs 240.8 kWh/m2 of kept-out sunlight over the two seasons. Most of the gap comes from fewer hours that need cooling in London (cooling benefit 180.1 vs 322.9 kWh/m2). London's heating penalty is not larger than Athens's, because its winter sun is weaker: there is less sunlight for the coating to reflect. Hottest hour of summer 2026 at the London reference point: 36.0 C (Open-Meteo). London reached 40 C in the July 2022 heatwave; that figure is from 2022, not 2026.
assumptions: The share of kept-out sunlight that would have reached the building interior depends on insulation and roof build-up; for a well-insulated roof it is small, so the kWh/m2 figures are an upper bound on building energy.
The summer gain is a real energy saving only in buildings that are actively cooled; in an unconditioned building it improves comfort but saves no energy.
Heating (15.5 C) and cooling (24.0 C) bases are standard degree-hour values, not fitted to these buildings.
An hour counts as heating or cooling demand when it crosses a base; the kept-out sunlight of that hour is counted in full, not scaled by how far the base is crossed.
method: Sunlight no longer absorbed = hourly global horizontal irradiation x (coated albedo - current median albedo), counted as benefit in hours above 24.0 C (cooling degree-hours) and as penalty in hours below 15.5 C (heating degree-hours), over summer and winter.
caveat: Rough estimate of sunlight absorbed at the roof surface, not of building energy use. See assumptions: the share that reaches the interior depends on insulation, and the summer figure only saves energy where the building is cooled.
